title: Watch This Shrimp-Like Fish Walk Backwards - Nautilus
gist: Sun Yat-sen University marine biologists used a submersible to film three deep-sea armored sea robin species in the South China Sea, confirming the fish 'walk' on independently controlled fin rays and, for the first time, capturing one species scuttling sideways and backwards.

insights.claim: Sea robins use specialized fin rays that emerge from their pectoral region as stiff, independently operated 'legs' to scuttle along the ocean floor.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Confirms an unusual locomotion mode, expanding understanding of how fish adapt to benthic life.
insights.locator: sea robins use their fin rays for walking

insights.claim: For the first time, researchers captured one species, Scalicus engyceros, scurrying sideways and even backwards along the seafloor.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: A novel behavioral observation that documents previously unseen locomotion in the species.
insights.locator: In a first, the team captured one species (Scalicus engyceros)

insights.claim: The armored sea robin's pectoral fins have evolved into rounded, skirt-like plates that fan out to provide balance while foraging.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Illustrates specialized morphology tied to seafloor foraging.
insights.locator: have evolved into rounded plates that fan out like a skirt

insights.claim: The sea robin's snout bears paired protrusions resembling tuning-fork prongs and rake-like appendages that help it sense and probe prey buried in sediment.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Details a sensory adaptation for hunting hidden prey in the deep-sea substrate.
insights.locator: unique snouts consisting of two paired protrusions

insights.claim: The fish reacted when researchers shone a light on them, indicating their eyes retain some light-sensing capacity despite living in an inky-black environment.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Suggests retained visual function in deep-sea species, informing sensory-ecology research.
insights.locator: this response indicates their eyes have retained some light-sensing activity

insights.claim: Marine biologists from Sun Yat-sen University filmed three sea robin species in the South China Sea using a submersible, publishing in Ocean-Land-Atmosphere Research.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Documents that submersible observation is unlocking behavior in hard-to-study deep-sea species.
insights.locator: Marine biologists from Sun Yat-sen University in China

insights.claim: Study author Han Tian argues these walking fish harbor far more novel behavioral and evolutionary adaptations than previously assumed, promising to reshape scientific views of deep-sea biodiversity.
insights.speaker: Jake Currie
insights.so_what: Signals extreme environments as a rich source of unique biological structures worth further study.
insights.quote: These walking fish harbor far more novel behavioral and evolutionary adaptations than previously assumed.
insights.locator: study author Han Tian said in a statement
